title: Printing Messages
narrative:
## Printing to the Console

Now that you know what a variable is, let's learn how to make your program talk! In XIOM, you use `io.println` to display messages on the screen.

### Your First Print

```xiom
io.println("Hello from XIOM!");
```

That's it! The text inside the double quotes is called a **string literal** (type `Str`). When your program runs, XIOM prints that message and moves the cursor to the next line.

### Printing Multiple Things

You can call `io.println` as many times as you want:

```xiom
io.println("Line one");
io.println("Line two");
```

Each call prints on its own line. This is what makes `println` different from just `println` prints and adds a newline.

### Printing Variables

You can combine strings with other values using `xiom.string` functions:

```xiom
let name = "Kilo";
io.println(string.format1("Hello, {}!", name));
```

### What's Happening?

When you call `io.println`, you're telling XIOM to send text to **standard output** — the console or terminal where your program runs. This is the simplest form of I/O (input/output) and every programming language has it.
tips: String literals always use double quotes `"like this"` in XIOM
You can print as many messages as you want — each `io.println` goes on a new line
Remember to add the semicolon `;` after each statement
Use `use xiom.string;` and `string.format1(...)` if you need to print variables inside strings
